title: Clay Four-Dimensional Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap

items.title: Four-dimensional Yang–Mills existence and mass gap
items.design_state: Step 1 authored draft; planned nonlogical record; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement: For every compact connected finite-dimensional Lie group $G$ whose Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is nonabelian and has no nonzero proper Lie ideals, construct a nontrivial four-dimensional quantum Yang–Mills theory with gauge group $G$. A Lie group is a smooth manifold with smooth multiplication and inversion, and its Lie algebra is its tangent space at the identity with the bracket induced by left-invariant vector fields. A Wightman realization means a theory satisfying the Wightman axioms: it supplies a Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, a unitary representation of translations and proper, orthochronous Lorentz isometries of Minkowski space $\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-,+,+,+)$, and local quantum fields as operator-valued tempered distributions on Schwartz test functions acting on a common dense invariant domain. The fields transform covariantly; gauge-invariant fields localized in regions whose points are spacelike separated, meaning $\eta(x-y,x-y)>0$, commute. Correlation functions are the vacuum expectation distributions of finite products of smeared fields. The self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ generating time translations has spectrum $\sigma(H)\subseteq[0,\infty)$, and there is a unique Poincaré-invariant vacuum vector $\Omega$ up to phase with $H\Omega=0$. Alternatively, a Euclidean construction gives Schwinger distributions, meaning Euclidean vacuum correlation distributions on $\mathbb R^4$, satisfying the Osterwalder–Schrader axioms (temperedness, Euclidean covariance, reflection positivity, permutation symmetry, and clustering) strongly enough for reconstruction of a Wightman theory. The required nontrivial gauge content includes local operator fields corresponding to gauge-invariant local polynomials in a smooth connection's curvature and its covariant derivatives, with short-distance correlations prescribed in a specified construction by asymptotic freedom (the perturbative prediction that the gauge coupling tends to zero at short distances) and perturbative renormalization. It includes a local stress-energy tensor whose charges generate spacetime translations and an operator product expansion, meaning a short-distance expansion of products of local fields in local fields. Here the curvature of a smooth local connection $A$ is $F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A\wedge A]$, and its covariant derivative on adjoint-valued forms is $D_A=d+[A,\cdot]$. The required mass gap is a finite number $\Delta>0$ such that $\sigma(H)\cap(0,\Delta)=\varnothing$, using units $c=\hbar=1$. Confinement is a separate question and is not part of this problem.

title: Clay Four-Dimensional Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap — Examples

items.title: Two global forms with the same simple Lie algebra
items.design_state: Step 1 authored draft; batch-local example expansion; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement: Let $\mathbb{H}$ be the real quaternion algebra with basis $1,i,j,k$, multiplication $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$, and norm $|a+bi+cj+dk|^2=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$. A Lie group is a finite-dimensional smooth manifold with smooth multiplication and inversion; its Lie algebra is its tangent space at the identity with the bracket induced by left-invariant vector fields. Let $SU(2)$ be the group of unit quaternions and $SO(3)$ the group of linear maps of $\operatorname{Im}\mathbb{H}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{i,j,k\}\cong\mathbb R^3$ preserving the Euclidean inner product and having determinant $+1$. A Lie algebra is simple if it is nonabelian and has no nonzero proper ideals. For this example, a compact simple gauge group means a compact connected Lie group with a simple Lie algebra. Its global form means the Lie group itself, including its central quotient, rather than only its Lie algebra. The kernel of a group homomorphism is the inverse image of the identity, and the center is the set of elements commuting with every group element. The map $\pi:SU(2)\to SO(3)$ defined by $\pi(q)x=qxq^{-1}$ is a surjective homomorphism with kernel $\{1,-1\}$; its differential identifies the simple Lie algebras of $SU(2)$ and $SO(3)$, while the groups are distinct. Therefore, a proof of a claim quantified over every compact simple gauge group at $SU(2)$ alone does not discharge the separate $SO(3)$ case.

references.title: Arthur Jaffe and Edward Witten, Quantum Yang-Mills Theory, §4, The Problem

items.title: A finite one-plaquette SU(2) regulator
items.design_state: Step 1 authored draft; batch-local example expansion; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be the finite oriented boundary cycle of a square, with four edges $e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4$ and one plaquette. Use the compact matrix group $G=SU(2)=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-\overline b&\overline a\end{pmatrix}:a,b\in\mathbb C,\ |a|^2+|b|^2=1\right\}$ in its defining two-dimensional representation. Assign one link variable $U_j\in G$ to each edge and set the ordered plaquette holonomy to $U_p=U_1U_2U_3^{-1}U_4^{-1}$. The group is the unit sphere $S^3$ in the $(a,b)$ coordinates; let $\mu$ be its normalized round surface measure. For $\beta\ge0$, define the dimensionless action $S_\beta(U)=\beta\left(1-\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}U_p\right)$ and partition function $Z_\beta=\int_{G^4}e^{-S_\beta(U)}\,d\mu^{\otimes4}(U)$. This finite graph integral satisfies $e^{-2\beta}\le Z_\beta\le1$, so it is finite and strictly positive. It has only four group variables and defines no continuum fields, no Wightman or Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction, and no Hamiltonian; it therefore does not solve the four-dimensional existence and mass-gap problem.
